readerTitle: Every investor's money comes with a finish line
caseNote: 가상 사례 (회계 서비스 회사, 카페, 비스트로) + 벤처 투자 수익 구조에 대한 일반적 관찰 · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 투자자의 기대는 그 사람이 자기 돈을 어떻게 돌려받아야 하는지에서 나온다. 돈을 받는 순간 그 목표가 내 사업의 목표가 된다.
misconception: 좋은 투자자는 좋은 사업이면 만족한다. 투자금은 갚을 필요가 없으니 공짜 자금이다.

sources.text: 벤처캐피털 수익 구조에 대한 일반적 설명 (소수의 투자가 펀드 수익 대부분을 만든다는 관찰, 펀드 존속 기간 약 10년)

factChecks.note: '벤처 펀드는 보통 약 10년 안에 출자자에게 돈을 돌려줘야 한다', '소수의 성공 투자가 나머지 손실을 메운다'는 업계의 일반적 설명입니다. 펀드마다 기간과 구조가 다르므로 카드에는 'roughly ten years', '10x 같은' 예시 표현으로만 적었습니다. 게시 전 표현을 다시 확인하세요.
7번 카드의 계약 조건(누가 먼저 돈을 받는지 등)은 특정 국가의 법률 조언이 되지 않도록 일반적으로만 적었습니다.

cards.title: Every investor's money comes with a finish line
body: Maya runs a 12-person bookkeeping firm for small companies. It's profitable and grows about 15% a year.
Over coffee, an investor offers $500,000 for 20% of the business. No monthly repayments. Friendly, smart, eager to help.
It feels like free fuel. It isn't. The money arrives with a destination someone else has already picked.

image.label: Two people at a café table, a check on the table pointing to a distant finish line
image.brief: 카페 테이블에 마주 앉은 두 사람. 테이블 위 수표에서 점선 길이 창밖 멀리 있는 결승선 깃발로 이어짐. 따뜻한 플랫 일러스트. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: What is this investor counting on?
body: The investor runs a fund that backs young, fast-growing companies. Maya plans to keep growing steadily and pay herself well.
What does the investor most likely expect in return?

options.text: A yearly share of the firm's profits
options.feedback: Some investors want exactly that. But a growth fund usually gets paid when its stake is sold, so yearly profit checks won't add up to what it needs.

options.text: To sell the 20% for many times $500,000 within several years
options.feedback: Right. The fund earns when it sells its stake, and it needs a big multiple to make its own numbers work. Next card shows the gap.

options.text: Nothing specific. They simply believe in Maya
options.feedback: Belief is real, but the fund owes money to its own investors. Assuming no expectations is how founders get surprised later.

cards.title: Run the investor's numbers.
body: In a growth fund, most bets return little. A few winners must cover all the rest. So each bet needs a real shot at something like **10x**.
cards.callout: A great business for Maya. A disappointing bet for the fund.
cards.softwareNote: The same gap hits software. A niche tool that can reach a few million in steady yearly revenue can be a wonderful business and still be too small for a fund that needs a $100M-plus outcome.

cards.title: Investors expect what their own deal requires.
body: **What investors expect** is set by how they themselves get paid: how much they need back, by when, and through what route.
A growth fund must return its own investors' money, plus more, within roughly ten years. So it needs a big sale or stock listing, and soon.
Once that fund owns part of your company, its target quietly becomes yours.

image.label: A chain of arrows: fund's backers to fund to company, each with a target
image.brief: 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 이어지는 화살표 사슬. "Fund's backers: want money back + more" → "Fund: needs a few big wins" → "Your company: must aim big and fast". 각 단계 위에 작은 목표 깃발.

cards.title: Three questions reveal any investor's expectations.
body: Ask these before you take anyone's money, including friends and family.
list: **How much back?** Ten times the money, double it, or a steady yearly return
**By when?** A fund with a deadline, a retiree who wants income now, or a patient family
**Paid how?** A sale of the company, a share of profits, dividends, or repayment with interest
cards.callout: If your business can't realistically reach their answers, the pressure lands on you.

cards.title: Unspoken expectations are the hardest ones.
body: A regular customer offers a café owner $80,000 toward a second location. No fund, no spreadsheet. Just "I believe in you."
Two years later, he asks why he hasn't seen a cent. He expected quarterly payouts. She planned to reinvest every dollar. Neither said so.
Small investors have expectations too. They're just invisible until they're disappointed.

cards.title: High expectations aren't the enemy. Mismatch is.
body: A fund's push for huge growth fits a business that can truly get huge. That founder may need both the money and the pressure.

Also, what people say over coffee matters less than what the signed deal says. The terms decide who gets paid first and what rights each investor holds. Read them with a qualified adviser before you sign.

cards.title: Now it's a bistro's second location.
body: Lena's bistro earns steady profits. She needs $200,000 to open a second site. She has no plan to build a chain or ever sell. Which money fits best?

options.text: A growth fund that wants a path to 100 locations within seven years
options.feedback: Plenty of money and ambition, but its finish line is a chain Lena doesn't want. Every decision would be pulled toward expansion.

options.text: A local investor who takes a share of profits until repaid 1.5 times, then a smaller share
options.feedback: Their payback comes from steady profits, which is exactly what the bistro produces. She gives up some cash for years, but the goals match.

options.text: A friend who says, "Pay me back whenever"
options.feedback: Flexible and kind, but "whenever" hides an expectation. Write down an amount and a rough timeline, or it may cost the friendship.

cards.title: Choose investors whose finish line matches yours.
body: Before taking money, ask how much they need back, by when, and how. Then ask honestly whether your business can get there.
**Try it today:** write one sentence about the business you want in seven years: its size, its profits, and whether you'd sell. Which kind of investor fits that picture?
